contraindications: Valproate in pregnancy: major teratogen and neurodevelopmental risk

output.formulary_status: Magnesium sulfate, labetalol, hydralazine, nifedipine, levetiracetam and lorazepam IV or oral: formulary.
interactions: Magnesium sulfate + nifedipine: additive hypotension; rare reports of potentiated neuromuscular blockade; may be used together with blood pressure and reflex monitoring
Magnesium sulfate + labetalol: no clinically significant interaction; labetalol can cause bradycardia and is avoided in asthma
Magnesium sulfate + lorazepam: additive respiratory and central nervous system depression; monitor respiratory rate and oxygen saturation
Magnesium sulfate + neuromuscular blockers: magnesium potentiates and prolongs blockade; relevant if general anaesthesia is needed for delivery
Valproate + lamotrigine: valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation and roughly doubles its concentration; raised risk of serious rash
Fosphenytoin or phenytoin + lamotrigine: enzyme induction increases lamotrigine clearance and lowers its concentration
output.proposed: Magnesium sulfate, antihypertensives (labetalol, hydralazine, nifedipine) and antiseizure options (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate) against current lamotrigine in pregnancy
output.summary: Magnesium sulfate adds to the hypotensive effect of nifedipine and to the respiratory depression of benzodiazepines, and is renally cleared. Valproate raises and phenytoin lowers lamotrigine concentrations. Levetiracetam has no interaction with these drugs.
warnings: Magnesium sulfate is renally excreted: with reduced renal function or oliguria, monitor serum magnesium, patellar reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output
Pregnancy increases lamotrigine clearance through glucuronidation; concentrations fall as pregnancy advances and rise after delivery

output.query: Eclampsia HELLP syndrome management delivery magnesium timing

results.finding: Magnesium sulfate, given as a 4-6 g intravenous load over 15 to 20 minutes followed by 1-2 g per hour, is the agent for prevention and treatment of eclamptic seizures; the maintenance dose is reduced with oliguria or raised creatinine [ACOG_PB222_2020].
In women with pre-eclampsia, magnesium sulfate roughly halved the risk of eclampsia compared with placebo [Magpie_2002].
Severe-range blood pressure (160 mmHg systolic or 110 mmHg diastolic or higher) is treated promptly with intravenous labetalol or hydralazine or oral immediate-release nifedipine [ACOG_PB222_2020].
Eclampsia and HELLP syndrome are indications for delivery once the mother is stabilized, regardless of gestational age [ACOG_PB222_2020].

output.summary: Eclampsia is managed with magnesium sulfate, treatment of severe-range blood pressure and delivery after maternal stabilization [ACOG_PB222_2020; Magpie_2002].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Lamotrigine 2.8, below range; platelets 88; AST 142 and ALT 118; LDH 684 with haptoglobin 14 and bilirubin 1.6; creatinine 1.1; urine protein:creatinine 4.2; INR 1.0; magnesium 1.7
action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function, lamotrigine level, coagulation and hemolysis markers
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; the lamotrigine level shows whether pregnancy has lowered it, and platelets, liver enzymes, LDH and coagulation identify HELLP and decide magnesium dosing and procedures [Brophy_2012; ACOG_PB222_2020].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Subtle bilateral parieto-occipital subcortical hypodensity; no hemorrhage
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast head CT after stabilization
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes hemorrhage, mass or edema that would change management, and must precede any LP [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Diffuse posterior-predominant 2-3 Hz delta slowing with a reactive background; no epileptiform discharges or electrographic seizures
action_criteria.label: Continuous video-EEG to exclude non-convulsive SE and monitor treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Persistent impaired consciousness after convulsive SE treated with lorazepam needs EEG to exclude non-convulsive SE; continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours [Brophy_2012]; terminology [ACNS_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral parieto-occipital and posterior frontal FLAIR hyperintensity with increased ADC and no restricted diffusion; no infarct or hemorrhage
action_criteria.label: MRI brain without contrast: PRES vs infarct, hemorrhage or venous thrombosis
action_criteria.rationale: New seizures with hypertension in pregnancy: MRI confirms vasogenic edema and excludes infarct, hemorrhage and venous infarction; gadolinium is avoided in pregnancy [Fugate_2015].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Patent dural venous sinuses and cortical veins without cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
action_criteria.label: MR venography to exclude cerebral venous thrombosis
action_criteria.rationale: Pregnancy raises the risk of cerebral venous thrombosis, which can present with seizures, headache and posterior edema like PRES [Fugate_2015].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Levetiracetam is interaction-free; valproate doubles and fosphenytoin lowers the lamotrigine level; magnesium with nifedipine lowers blood pressure further
action_criteria.label: Drug-interaction check: magnesium sulfate, antihypertensives and second-line ASM against lamotrigine in pregnancy
action_criteria.rationale: Magnesium interacts with nifedipine and benzodiazepines and is renally cleared, and valproate and fosphenytoin change lamotrigine levels, which decides the second-line ASM [ESETT_2019; ACOG_PB222_2020].

action_criteria.label: Literature: eclampsia and HELLP management
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step [ACOG_PB222_2020].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not use valproate in pregnancy: it is a major teratogen and doubles the lamotrigine level.
Do not use benzodiazepines or phenytoin in place of magnesium sulfate to prevent recurrent eclamptic seizures [ACOG_PB222_2020].
Do not perform a lumbar puncture: it is not indicated, because the seizures are explained by eclampsia, and platelets are 88 x10^9/L in HELLP.
Do not postpone delivery beyond maternal stabilization in eclampsia with HELLP, whatever the gestational age [ACOG_PB222_2020].
Do not use ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers in pregnancy.
required_recommendations: Give IV magnesium sulfate 4-6 g over 15 to 20 minutes, then 1-2 g/h, at the lower maintenance rate because creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL, monitoring patellar reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output and serum magnesium [Magpie_2002; ACOG_PB222_2020].
Treat the severe-range blood pressure (168/104) promptly with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine or oral immediate-release nifedipine [ACOG_PB222_2020].

Load a second-line ASM for the breakthrough epilepsy: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), and avoid valproate because it is teratogenic and doubles the lamotrigine level, and fosphenytoin because it lowers the lamotrigine level [ESETT_2019].
Continue lamotrigine and increase the dose with neurology, guided by repeat levels, because pregnancy increases its clearance.
Plan delivery with obstetrics once she is stabilized (eclampsia with HELLP at 28 weeks); antenatal corticosteroids may be given but must not delay delivery [ACOG_PB222_2020].
Continuous fetal heart rate monitoring, with obstetric and neonatal teams involved.
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].

avoided_actions.rationale: LP is not indicated: the seizures are explained by eclampsia, and platelets are 88 x10^9/L in HELLP.
No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

accepted: Convulsive status epilepticus from concurrent eclampsia with HELLP syndrome and breakthrough epilepsy from subtherapeutic lamotrigine at 28 weeks gestation

differential.key_features: BP 168/104, proteinuria 4.2, HELLP labs and PRES on MRI establish eclampsia; the lamotrigine level of 2.8, below range in known epilepsy, makes a concurrent breakthrough likely, so eclampsia alone is an incomplete explanation

differential.diagnosis: Breakthrough epilepsy from subtherapeutic lamotrigine alone
differential.key_features: Lamotrigine 2.8 below range, but severe-range hypertension, proteinuria, hemolysis, raised transaminases, thrombocytopenia and posterior vasogenic edema cannot be explained by epilepsy
Hemolysis, thrombocytopenia and seizures overlap with HELLP; platelets 88 (TTP usually below 30) with marked transaminase rise, hypertension and proteinuria favor HELLP
Pregnancy raises the risk; MR venography shows patent sinuses and cortical veins, and MRI shows no venous infarct or hemorrhage
CT shows no hemorrhage and MRI shows no restricted diffusion or blood

key_clinical_evidence: Eclampsia is treated with IV magnesium sulfate first, not with benzodiazepines alone
Pregnancy increases lamotrigine clearance, so levels fall as pregnancy advances
LP is not indicated, and HELLP thrombocytopenia adds risk
Delivery after maternal stabilization is the definitive treatment for eclampsia with HELLP

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: With LDH 684, low haptoglobin and raised bilirubin, these labs define HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) in pregnancy-associated hypertension, not primary hepatitis or a primary coagulopathy (INR and fibrinogen normal)

patient.chief_complaint: Pregnant patient (28 weeks) brought by ambulance after a 10-minute generalized convulsion stopped with IV lorazepam en route; not waking up

medications.indication: Generalized epilepsy (dose increased in pregnancy per neurology)

past_medical_history: Generalized epilepsy (since age 12, well-controlled until pregnancy)

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Kim is a 35-year-old woman at 28 weeks gestation with generalized epilepsy well-controlled on lamotrigine who is brought by ambulance, with her husband, after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She was eating dinner when she suddenly lost consciousness and began convulsing. Paramedics found her still convulsing about 10 minutes after onset and gave lorazepam 4 mg IV, which stopped the convulsion; she has not regained consciousness since. She had not had a seizure for 2 years before this pregnancy. Her neurologist increased lamotrigine to 300 mg twice daily during pregnancy after noting declining levels. She had a lamotrigine level drawn 2 weeks ago which was 4.2 mcg/mL (low end of therapeutic). Her husband reports that her home blood pressure readings had risen to 150-160/95-100 over the past 3 days, and that she complained of a headache and blurred vision since the morning.
